subtitle: Can a cheap probe tell when a question needs a multi-agent system?
premise_title: The premise fails: MAS does not beat CoT-SC
premise_note: Strict grading, all 387 calibration runs per system. Part of the gap is MAS writing wordy answers: under a lenient check (gold answer stated inside a short answer) the gap shrinks to -3.9 points and is no longer significant (p = 0.26). Either way MAS is never better, so H1 is not supported on Qwen2.5-3B.
results_title: The gate keeps accuracy at 39% fewer tokens
results_note: The calibrated gate (MLP) escalated 1% of test tasks, so it behaves almost exactly like CoT-SC-only. That is the right call when MAS rarely helps. The rule-based gate escalates 69% of tasks and pays for it in both accuracy and tokens.
oracle_text: With these two systems even a perfect gate would escalate only 6% of questions: CoT-SC already answers most of them, and MAS fixes few of the rest. The learned gate found that ceiling's shape, stopping almost always.
ablation_text: Consistency carries the logistic gate: removing it costs 3 points and cuts escalations from 9% to 3%. No other single feature changes it. With only 12% ESCALATE labels, the gate has little to learn beyond the probe's own agreement.
conclusion: On Qwen2.5-3B, MAS is less accurate than CoT-SC and costs 26% more, so the gate's best move is to stop. It does: CoT-SC accuracy at 39% fewer tokens than Always-MAS. The next test is a stronger model, where MAS may finally earn its cost.
conclusion_note: RQ1: yes against Always-MAS, but only because MAS is not worth running here. RQ2: higher k raises validation savings without changing accuracy. RQ3: probe consistency is the only feature the logistic gate depends on. H1: not supported.
